triage.name: Canker Sores
triage.reason: Recurrent painful oral ulcers with a recognizable history and exam; differential includes herpes, Behçet, and drug causes, so it works as a clinic case.

presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: Often begins in childhood or adolescence and recurs for years
More common in higher socioeconomic groups and in non-smokers

risk_factors.text: Family history of recurrent aphthous ulcers
Local trauma to the mouth (biting the lip or cheek, dental work, hard brushing)
Foods that trigger attacks (chocolate, nuts, citrus, acidic or spicy foods)

comorbidities: Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis)
Nutritional deficiency (iron, folate, vitamin B12, zinc)
family_history: Recurrent canker sores in a parent or sibling
social_history: Often worse around exams, deadlines or other stressful periods

chief_complaints.text: I have a sore in my mouth that really hurts
It hurts when I eat or drink
I keep getting these sores over and over

hpi.onset: Sudden; many patients feel a burning or tingling spot a day or two before the sore appears
hpi.duration: Sores last about 7–14 days and heal without scarring; crops recur a few times a year
hpi.progression: Starts as a small red tender spot, then becomes a shallow ulcer with a gray-white center and a red rim; pain peaks in the first few days and then slowly fades as it heals
hpi.location: Inside the lips, inside the cheeks, on the tongue, floor of the mouth, soft palate or back of the throat; movable lining of the mouth rather than the gums or hard palate
hpi.radiation: Pain can spread to the jaw or ear on the same side with larger sores
hpi.quality: Burning, raw, stinging pain; the sore itself is a shallow, round or oval ulcer
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; often 5–8/10 at its worst, enough to make eating and talking uncomfortable
hpi.timing: Constant pain that is worst with eating, drinking, talking or brushing teeth
aggravating: Touching the sore with the tongue
relieving: Pain relievers such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen

associated_symptoms.text: Tingling or burning at the spot before the sore appears
Pain that makes it hard to eat or drink
Drooling or avoiding food in children
Mild swelling or tenderness of the nearby lymph nodes
Low-grade fever in children with many sores

pertinent_negatives: Sores on the outside of the lips or around the mouth
Blisters that break and crust over
Sores on the gums, hard palate or top of the tongue
Skin rash, joint pain or diarrhea
New medicines started before the sores appeared

argues_against: Systemic illness such as Behçet syndrome or an infection

positives.text: Pain with eating, drinking or talking

negatives: Sores on the outside of the lips

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children can't describe the sore; they present with crying, refusing to eat or drink, drooling and irritability, and may have a low-grade fever with several sores at once.
Sores are larger, more numerous, slower to heal and more likely to be caused by something other than ordinary recurrent aphthous ulcers.
A new mouth ulcer in an older adult is less likely to be simple recurrent aphthous ulcers and more often needs a search for medication, nutritional or malignant causes.
missing_classic_features: Long history of recurrent crops since youth

general.mild: Well-appearing, comfortable between episodes of eating or talking
general.moderate: Well-appearing but visibly uncomfortable when speaking or swallowing; may avoid talking
general.severe: Ill-appearing, hesitant to speak or swallow, may drool or refuse food
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, dehydrated, lethargic, unable to swallow

findings.maneuver: Inspect the entire oral cavity with a light and tongue blade, including the inside of the lips, buccal mucosa, tongue, floor of the mouth, soft palate and posterior pharynx
findings.finding: One or more shallow, round or oval ulcers with a gray-white or yellow fibrinous center and an erythematous halo on the movable oral mucosa

findings.maneuver: Estimate the diameter of the ulcer relative to a known reference (e.g., millimeters on a tongue blade)
findings.finding: Most ulcers are small (under 1 cm); larger ulcers over 1 cm suggest major aphthous ulcers or another cause

findings.maneuver: Gently palpate the ulcer and surrounding mucosa with a gloved finger or cotton swab
findings.finding: Marked tenderness of the ulcer and surrounding mucosa; the ulcer is soft and not indurated

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral mucosa for vesicles, bullae or intact blisters
findings.finding: No vesicles or intact blisters; lesions are ulcers from the start

findings.maneuver: Inspect the gingiva and hard palate
findings.finding: Gingiva and hard palate are spared; lesions are on movable mucosa

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lips, perioral skin and vermilion border
findings.finding: No crusted vesicles or erosions on the outer lips or around the mouth

findings.maneuver: Palpate the cervical lymph node chains bilaterally
Measure temperature and assess for systemic signs
Inspect the eyes for redness, discharge or photophobia
findings.finding: No conjunctival injection, uveitis or ocular discharge

findings.maneuver: Ask about and, when indicated, inspect the genitalia for ulcers
Inspect the skin for rash, pustules or nodules
findings.finding: No rash, erythema nodosum or folliculitis

findings.maneuver: Assess mucous membranes, skin turgor and capillary refill
findings.finding: Dry mucous membranes and delayed capillary refill in patients who cannot drink because of pain

labs.caveat: Low ferritin supports iron deficiency, a recognized contributor to recurrent aphthous ulcers.
Low B12 is a treatable cause of recurrent mouth ulcers.
Low folate is another treatable nutritional cause.
Mildly elevated only when a systemic inflammatory condition such as Behçet syndrome or inflammatory bowel disease is present; normal in simple recurrent aphthous ulcers.
Usually normal; elevation suggests an underlying systemic inflammatory disorder.

initial.why: Looks for anemia or a hematologic abnormality that would suggest a systemic cause
Screens for iron deficiency, a common and treatable trigger

supporting.only_if: systemic symptoms such as fever, weight loss, genital or eye involvement, or diarrhea are present
systemic symptoms such as fever, weight loss, genital or eye involvement, or diarrhea are present

not_indicated.why: No role unless vesicles, perioral crusting or gingival involvement suggest herpes simplex
Not routine; consider only with atypical, severe or nonhealing ulcers or other risk factors
Not indicated for typical small recurrent ulcers; reserve for persistent, indurated or nonhealing lesions concerning for malignancy or a blistering disease

decision_points: Typical small recurrent ulcers on movable mucosa with a gray-white center and red halo need no testing beyond a nutritional screen
Order ESR/CRP and consider Behçet syndrome or inflammatory bowel disease when genital ulcers, eye inflammation, skin lesions or GI symptoms are present
Biopsy any ulcer that persists beyond 3 weeks, is indurated, or fails to heal, to exclude malignancy
Review new medications (NSAIDs, methotrexate, nicorandil) as a possible trigger

differential.name: Herpes simplex virus infection (primary gingivostomatitis or recurrent herpes labialis)
differential.why_considered: Painful oral lesions are the most common reason patients present, and herpes is the classic mimic of aphthous ulcers.
differential.trigger: Vesicles or blisters that rupture and crust, involvement of the gingiva, hard palate or outer lips, or a febrile prodrome

history: Prodrome of tingling or burning followed by a cluster of blisters
Fever, malaise and refusal to eat in primary infection
Sores on the outside of the lips or around the mouth
Recurrences at the same site
exam: Vesicles or intact blisters that break and crust
Lesions on the hard palate or attached gingiva
labs: Positive HSV PCR from an unroofed vesicle

differential.name: Behçet syndrome
differential.why_considered: Recurrent oral ulcers are the cardinal feature, and missing the systemic disease delays treatment of a potentially sight-threatening and life-threatening condition.
differential.trigger: Recurrent oral ulcers plus genital ulcers, eye inflammation, skin lesions or a positive pathergy test

history: Recurrent genital ulcers
Eye redness, pain or blurred vision
Skin sores or acne-like lesions
Joint pain or swelling
Family history or origin in an endemic region
exam: Erythema nodosum or folliculitis-like skin lesions
labs: Elevated ESR and CRP during flares
imaging: MR or CT angiography if vascular involvement is suspected

differential.name: Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis)
differential.why_considered: Oral aphthous ulcers are a common extraintestinal manifestation and can precede GI symptoms.

history: Chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain or blood in stool
Weight loss and fatigue
Perianal fistulas or abscesses
exam: Perianal skin tags, fistulas or fissures
Cobblestone mucosa or linear ulcers on oral exam
imaging: Terminal ileum thickening or skip lesions on CT or MR enterography
Colonoscopy with biopsy showing transmural inflammation

differential.name: Celiac disease
differential.why_considered: Recurrent aphthous ulcers are a recognized presentation of celiac disease, often with subtle GI symptoms.

history: Chronic diarrhea, bloating or weight loss
Iron-deficiency anemia
Family history of celiac disease
imaging: Small bowel biopsy showing villous atrophy

differential.name: Nutritional deficiency (iron, folate, vitamin B12, zinc)
differential.why_considered: Deficiencies are common, treatable causes of recurrent mouth ulcers and are part of the standard workup.

history: Restricted or unusual diet
Heavy menstrual bleeding
Bariatric surgery or malabsorption
Paresthesias or glossitis
exam: Decreased vibration or position sense with B12 deficiency

differential.name: Medication-induced oral ulceration
differential.why_considered: NSAIDs, methotrexate, nicorandil and some chemotherapies can cause oral ulcers that mimic aphthous ulcers.

history: New medication started before the sores appeared
Dose escalation of a known culprit drug
Ulcers resolve when the drug is stopped
exam: Ulcers may be larger or atypical in location

differential.name: Squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity
differential.why_considered: A nonhealing oral ulcer can be malignant, and delay in diagnosis worsens outcomes.
differential.trigger: An ulcer that persists beyond 3 weeks, is indurated, or is associated with tobacco or alcohol use

history: Tobacco or heavy alcohol use
Ulcer present for more than 3 weeks
Progressive pain, dysphagia or weight loss
History of head and neck cancer
exam: Fixed, hard lymph node in the neck
Lesion on the lateral tongue, floor of mouth or soft palate
imaging: Biopsy showing invasive squamous cell carcinoma

severity.mild: One or two small ulcers under 1 cm on movable mucosa; mild pain that does not limit eating or drinking; no systemic symptoms; heals in 7–14 days without scarring
severity.moderate: Several ulcers or a larger ulcer causing significant pain that limits eating, drinking or talking; may have tender cervical lymph nodes; no dehydration or systemic illness
severity.severe: Numerous or large (over 1 cm) ulcers, or continuous crops that interfere with oral intake; dehydration or weight loss may develop; consider major aphthous ulcers or an underlying systemic cause
severity.critical: Not applicable; canker sores are not life-threatening, but severe cases can cause dehydration, especially in children, which requires urgent supportive care

red_flags.finding: Ulcer persisting beyond 3 weeks or failing to heal
red_flags.meaning: Needs biopsy to exclude malignancy or a blistering disease

red_flags.finding: Indurated, rolled or everted ulcer edges
Genital ulcers, eye redness or pain, or skin lesions
red_flags.meaning: Suggests Behçet syndrome or another systemic inflammatory disease

red_flags.finding: Fever, weight loss, diarrhea or blood in stool
red_flags.meaning: Suggests inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease or infection

red_flags.finding: Inability to eat or drink, drooling, or signs of dehydration
red_flags.meaning: Requires urgent supportive care, especially in children

red_flags.finding: New medication started before the ulcers appeared
red_flags.meaning: Consider drug-induced ulceration and review the medication list

complications.name: Secondary bacterial infection of the ulcer
clues: Increasing pain, swelling or purulent discharge

special_populations.differences: Young children cannot describe the sore and present with crying, refusing to eat or drink, drooling and irritability; dehydration is the main concern and may require urgent care.
Ulcers are larger, more numerous and slower to heal; consider herpes simplex, cytomegalovirus, fungal infection or drug-induced mucositis rather than simple recurrent aphthous ulcers.
A new oral ulcer is less likely to be simple recurrent aphthous ulcers; evaluate for medication effects, nutritional deficiency and malignancy, and biopsy nonhealing lesions.
Hormonal changes can trigger or worsen recurrent aphthous ulcers; treatment is limited to topical agents and acetaminophen, avoiding systemic agents that are unsafe in pregnancy.

key_questions.question: Where in your mouth is the sore, and what does it look like?
key_questions.looking_for: Inside the lips, cheeks, tongue, floor of mouth or soft palate; a shallow round or oval ulcer with a gray-white center and a red rim on movable mucosa

key_questions.question: How long has this sore been there, and have you had sores like this before?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent crops over months to years, each lasting about 7–14 days and healing without scarring; a first or nonhealing ulcer raises concern for another cause

key_questions.question: Did you notice any tingling or burning before the sore appeared?
key_questions.looking_for: A brief burning or tingling spot a day or two before the ulcer, typical of aphthous ulcers

key_questions.question: What makes the pain worse, and what helps?
key_questions.looking_for: Worse with hot, spicy, salty or acidic foods, chewing, talking and brushing; better with cold foods and topical gels or rinses

key_questions.question: How much is this affecting your eating and drinking?
key_questions.looking_for: Pain that limits oral intake; refusal to eat or drink, drooling or weight loss suggests dehydration, especially in children

key_questions.question: Have you had a fever, felt unwell, or lost weight?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in simple aphthous ulcers; present suggests a systemic illness or infection

key_questions.question: Have you had sores on your genitals, or any eye redness, pain or blurred vision?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; genital ulcers or eye inflammation suggest Behçet syndrome

key_questions.question: Any diarrhea, blood in the stool, or abdominal pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests inflammatory bowel disease or celiac disease

key_questions.question: Have you had any skin rash, joint pain or swelling?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests a systemic inflammatory condition such as Behçet syndrome or inflammatory bowel disease

key_questions.question: Have you started any new medicines recently?
key_questions.looking_for: NSAIDs, methotrexate, nicorandil or chemotherapy started before the sores appeared, suggesting drug-induced ulceration

key_questions.question: Does anyone else in your family get sores like these?
key_questions.looking_for: A parent or sibling with recurrent canker sores, supporting a familial tendency

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or use tobacco, and how much alcohol do you drink?
key_questions.looking_for: Tobacco or heavy alcohol use raises concern for oral squamous cell carcinoma, especially with a nonhealing ulcer

key_questions.question: Has this ulcer lasted more than three weeks, or does it feel hard or raised?
key_questions.looking_for: An ulcer persisting beyond 3 weeks or with indurated, rolled edges needs biopsy to exclude malignancy

reasoning_points: Recurrent crops of painful shallow oral ulcers on movable mucosa, each lasting about 7–14 days and healing without scarring
A gray-white or yellow fibrinous center with an erythematous halo, without vesicles or blisters
Sparing of the gingiva, hard palate and outer lips, which argues against herpes simplex
No fever, systemic symptoms, genital ulcers, eye inflammation, skin rash or GI symptoms to suggest Behçet syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease or infection
No new culprit medication such as an NSAID, methotrexate or nicorandil
Nutritional screen for iron, folate and vitamin B12 deficiency as treatable contributors
An ulcer persisting beyond 3 weeks, indurated, or nonhealing requires biopsy to exclude malignancy

easy: Young adult with a long history of recurrent small painful mouth ulcers
Classic shallow ulcer with a gray-white center and red halo on the buccal mucosa or inside the lip
No fever, no systemic symptoms, no genital or eye involvement
Heals without scarring in under two weeks
medium: Child who cannot describe the sore and presents with crying, drooling and refusal to eat
Patient with several ulcers at once and tender cervical lymph nodes
Patient with a history of iron-deficiency anemia or heavy menstrual bleeding
Ulcer triggered by recent dental work, braces or a new toothpaste
hard: Older adult with a new, nonhealing oral ulcer concerning for malignancy
Immunocompromised patient with large, numerous or slow-healing ulcers suggesting herpes, CMV or drug-induced mucositis
Patient with recurrent oral ulcers plus genital ulcers or eye inflammation suggesting Behçet syndrome
Patient with oral ulcers and diarrhea or weight loss suggesting inflammatory bowel disease or celiac disease
Patient on methotrexate or nicorandil with new oral ulcers suggesting drug-induced ulceration
